content: Infants under 12 months of age have been associated with adverse outcomes, including fatalities, linked to the use of cough and cold medications. Medical examiners or coroners have determined these medications to be the underlying cause of death in certain cases. These incidents highlight the critical importance of clinicians exercising caution when prescribing, and caregivers being vigilant when administering, cough and cold medications to children under the age of 2 years. For further information, visit the FDA website. Acetaminophen is a medication used to alleviate mild to moderate pain caused by conditions such as headaches, muscle aches, menstrual cramps, colds, sore throats, toothaches, backaches, and reactions to vaccinations. It is also effective in reducing fever. Additionally, acetaminophen may be used to manage the pain associated with osteoarthritis, a condition resulting from the breakdown of joint cartilage. This medication belongs to the class of drugs known as analgesics and antipyretics. It functions by altering the body’s perception of pain and by lowering body temperature. Acetaminophen is available in various forms, including tablets, chewable tablets, capsules, liquid suspensions, concentrated liquid drops, extended-release tablets, and orally disintegrating tablets. It can be taken orally, with or without food. It is also available as a rectal suppository. While acetaminophen can be purchased without a prescription, a doctor may prescribe it for specific conditions. Always follow the instructions on the package or prescription label carefully. If you have any questions, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Take acetaminophen exactly as directed, and do not exceed the recommended dosage, as this can lead to liver damage. When administering acetaminophen to children, refer to the dosage chart on the package to determine the appropriate amount based on the child’s weight or age. Never give children acetaminophen products intended for adults. If you are unsure about the correct dosage, consult your child’s doctor. Extended-release tablets should be swallowed whole and not split, chewed, crushed, or dissolved. Orally disintegrating tablets should be placed in the mouth to dissolve or be chewed before swallowing. Shake liquid suspensions and drops well before use to ensure even distribution of the medication. Use the provided measuring device to accurately measure each dose. Do not mix concentrated drops with baby formula. For rectal suppositories, follow proper insertion techniques, including removing the wrapper, moistening the tip with water, and inserting it into the rectum as directed. Discontinue acetaminophen and contact your doctor if symptoms worsen, new or unexpected symptoms develop, the painful area becomes red or swollen, pain persists for more than 10 days, or fever worsens or lasts longer than 3 days. For children, stop use and consult a doctor if new symptoms arise, such as redness or swelling at the painful site, pain lasting more than 5 days, or fever persisting beyond 3 days. Do not give acetaminophen to a child with a severe sore throat accompanied by fever, headache, rash, nausea, or vomiting, as these may indicate a more serious condition requiring immediate medical attention. Acetaminophen may also be used in combination with aspirin and caffeine to relieve migraine headaches. It may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Before taking acetaminophen, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, any other medications, or any ingredients in the product. Avoid taking multiple products containing acetaminophen simultaneously, as many prescription and over-the-counter medications include it in combination with other drugs. Always read package labels or consult your healthcare provider to ensure you are not taking more than one acetaminophen-containing product at a time. Inform your doctor about all medications, vitamins, supplements, or herbal products you are currently taking, especially anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), isoniazid, seizure medications (e.g., carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin), pain relievers, fever reducers, cough and cold medications, and phenothiazines. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. If you have any serious medical conditions, are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you consume three or more alcoholic beverages daily, consult your doctor about the safe use of acetaminophen. Additionally, if you have phenylketonuria (PKU), be aware that some brands of chewable tablets may contain phenylalanine. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking acetaminophen. If you miss a dose and are taking acetaminophen regularly, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Acetaminophen may cause side effects, some of which can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience symptoms such as rash, hives, itching, swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, hoarseness, or difficulty breathing or swallowing. Report any unusual problems to your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store acetaminophen in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture. Discard expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or is not breathing. Seek immediate medical attention even if no symptoms are present, as overdose can cause severe complications. Symptoms of overdose may include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, sweating, extreme fatigue, unusual bleeding or bruising, pain in the upper right abdomen, yellowing of the skin or eyes, and flu-like symptoms. Before undergoing any laboratory tests, inform your doctor and laboratory personnel that you are taking acetaminophen. If you have any questions about this medication, consult your pharmacist.
